Getting started with rk8s

Source: vignettes/getting-started.Rmd
getting-started.Rmd

This guide walks through the parts of rk8s you’ll use most: connecting, the verbs, watches and informers, exec and port-forward, leader election, and the generated API underneath. None of the code runs when the vignette is built, since it needs a cluster. The examples assume a pod called nginx-abc and, once you get to the apply section, a Deployment called nginx.

Installing 

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("ian-flores/rk8s")

Connecting 

library(rk8s)
k <- kube()                                   # $KUBECONFIG or ~/.kube/config
# k <- kube(context = "my-dev")
# k <- kube(config_file = "~/configs/prod.yaml")
# k <- kube(namespace = "my-app")             # override the context namespace

From a pod running as a ServiceAccount:

k <- kube(client = ApiClient$new(load_incluster_config()))

kube() calls load_kube_config(), which handles the kubeconfig features you’re likely to meet. KUBECONFIG can list several files; they’re merged and the first definition of a name wins. Each context’s default namespace is used. Users can authenticate with a token or token file, basic auth, or a client certificate (inline, or a file path relative to the kubeconfig it appears in). Exec plugins work too: EKS’s aws-iam-authenticator, GKE’s gke-gcloud-auth-plugin, AKS’s kubelogin and any OIDC helper. So does the older oidc auth-provider, including refreshing its token. Clusters can set proxy-url, tls-server-name and insecure-skip-tls-verify.

If the API server throttles you (429), the request is retried whatever its method. Server errors (500 to 504) and dropped connections are retried only for reads, since retrying a write could apply it twice. Configuration$max_retries sets the limit; the default is 3.

The verbs

You can refer to a resource type in several ways:

  • by kind or alias: "pod", "pods", "po", "deploy", "svc", "ing", "crd" and so on
  • with a name attached: "deployment/nginx"
  • by API version and kind: "apps/v1:Deployment"
  • as a vector: c("apps/v1", "Deployment")

Getting and listing 

kube_get(k, "pods", namespace = "default")              # list
kube_get(k, "pod", "nginx-abc")                          # single
kube_get(k, "deployment/nginx")                          # alt syntax
kube_get(k, "pods", label_selector = "app=nginx")
kube_get(k, "apps/v1:Deployment", "nginx")               # explicit GVK

You get back an rk8s_object for a single resource and an rk8s_list for a collection. kube_list() always returns a list, and pages through large collections for you. To look at a list as a table, use as.data.frame():

pods <- kube_get(k, "pods")
head(as.data.frame(pods))
#>     namespace                    name kind     age   status
#> 1     default                  nginx-1  Pod    12m  Running
#> 2     default                  nginx-2  Pod    12m  Running
#> 3 kube-system          coredns-abc-xyz  Pod      4h  Running

Applying

kube_apply() does a server-side apply. Give it a file, a YAML or JSON string, an R list, or one of the generated model objects. A YAML string can hold several documents, and each goes to the right endpoint:

# From a file
kube_apply(k, "deployment.yaml")

# From an R list (the most natural form for programmatic generation)
kube_apply(k, list(
  apiVersion = "v1", kind = "ConfigMap",
  metadata = list(name = "demo"),
  data = list(hello = "world")
))

# From a multi-doc YAML string
kube_apply(k, "
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata: {name: demo-cm}
data: {greeting: hello}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: {name: demo-svc}
spec:
  selector: {app: demo}
  ports: [{port: 80, targetPort: 8080}]
")

# Force-take ownership of conflicting fields (server-side apply force):
kube_apply(k, "deployment.yaml", force = TRUE)

Changes are recorded under the field manager "rk8s" unless you pass field_manager.

Scaling, logs, watching and deleting 

kube_scale(k, "deployment", "nginx", replicas = 5)
kube_scale(k, "statefulset/postgres", replicas = 3)

cat(kube_logs(k, "nginx-abc", tail = 50))
kube_logs(k, "nginx-abc", container = "sidecar", follow = TRUE)

w <- kube_watch(k, "pods",
  on_event = function(type, obj) {
    message(type, " ", obj$metadata$name)
    TRUE  # keep watching; return FALSE to stop
  },
  timeout_seconds = 30
)
w$end_reason   # "stop", "timeout" or "gone" (resourceVersion too old)

kube_delete(k, "pod", "nginx-abc")
kube_delete(k, "deployment/nginx", grace_period = 0)

timeout_seconds is measured on the clock. The API server ends watches on its own schedule; rk8s reconnects when that happens and returns once your time is up.

Custom resources

Custom resources need no setup. rk8s finds them through API discovery, so the verbs take any apiVersion and kind the cluster knows about. A small reconcile loop over a made-up Foo resource looks like this:

foos <- kube_list(k, "example.com/v1:Foo", namespace = "default")
for (f in foos$items) {
  if (is.null(f$status$ready) || !isTRUE(f$status$ready)) {
    kube_apply(k, list(
      apiVersion = "example.com/v1", kind = "Foo",
      metadata = list(name = f$metadata$name),
      status = list(ready = TRUE)
    ))
  }
}

Informers

Listing everything on every pass gets expensive. An informer lists once, then keeps a local copy current from a watch and calls your handlers as things change. If the watch falls too far behind, the API server answers 410 Gone; the informer then lists again, works out what changed while it was away, and fires on_delete for anything that disappeared.

inf <- Informer$new(
  k$client,
  resource_path = "/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods",
  object_from_list = V1Pod$from_list
)
inf$add_event_handler(
  on_add    = function(obj) message("add: ", obj$metadata$name),
  on_update = function(old, new) {
    if (!identical(old$status$phase, new$status$phase))
      message(new$metadata$name, ": ",
              old$status$phase, " -> ", new$status$phase)
  },
  on_delete = function(obj) message("gone: ", obj$metadata$name)
)
inf$run(stop_seconds = 120)

pods <- inf$lister()
pods$get("nginx-abc", namespace = "default")   # cache lookup, no API call
pods$list()

Exec and port-forward

pod_exec() runs a command and gives you its output and exit code:

r <- pod_exec(k$client, "default", "nginx-abc", c("ls", "-la", "/"))
cat(r$stdout)
r$exit_code

# With stdin
pod_exec(k$client, "default", "nginx-abc", "cat", stdin_data = "hi\n")$stdout

For something interactive, pod_exec_open() returns a PodExecSession you can write to with write_stdin() and read from with on_stdout(). Output only arrives while wait() or pump() is running.

pod_port_forward() works like kubectl port-forward:

fwd <- pod_port_forward(k$client, "default", "nginx-abc", remote_port = 80)
httr2::request(paste0("http://127.0.0.1:", fwd$port)) |> httr2::req_perform()
fwd$close()

Both need the nanonext package. They check the API server’s certificate against the CA in your kubeconfig (or the system’s, if the kubeconfig has none), and they log in with a token. Kind, minikube and kubeadm give their default user a client certificate and no token, so with those you’ll get an error until you use a token instead:

# kubectl create serviceaccount rk8s-dev
# kubectl create clusterrolebinding rk8s-dev --clusterrole=edit \
#   --serviceaccount=default:rk8s-dev
cfg <- load_kube_config()
cfg$api_key <- list(authorization = paste(
  "Bearer", system("kubectl create token rk8s-dev", intern = TRUE)))
k <- kube(client = ApiClient$new(cfg))

Leader election

When you run more than one replica of a controller, you want only one of them doing the work:

run_as_leader(
  k$client,
  lease_name = "my-controller",
  lease_namespace = "kube-system",
  identity = paste0(Sys.info()[["nodename"]], "-", Sys.getpid()),
  on_started_leading = function(leader) {
    message("leading")
    repeat {
      leader$check()      # signals once leadership is lost
      reconcile_once()
      Sys.sleep(5)
    }
  },
  on_stopped_leading = function() message("stopped leading")
)

While your callback runs, a background process (started with callr) keeps renewing the lease. If another replica takes the lease, or renewals keep failing, the next leader$check() signals an rk8s_leadership_lost condition. run_as_leader() catches it, releases the lease and calls on_stopped_leading. Call leader$check() at least once per renew_deadline_seconds; that’s what keeps two replicas from acting as leader at the same time. If you’d rather test than be interrupted, leader$is_leader() returns TRUE or FALSE.

Errors

When the API server returns an error, rk8s signals an rk8s_api_error condition. Its exception field is an ApiException holding the HTTP status, reason, headers and the parsed Status object.

pod <- tryCatch(
  kube_get(k, "pod", "nope"),
  rk8s_api_error = function(e) {
    if (e$exception$status == 404L) NULL else stop(e)
  }
)

The generated API

The verbs cover common work. For everything else there are the generated classes, one per API group and version, with methods named after the official Python client’s. They all take the session’s ApiClient:

# Typed:
core <- CoreV1Api$new(k$client)
pods <- V1PodList$from_list(core$list_pod_for_all_namespaces())

# Or build a typed model explicitly:
dep <- V1Deployment$new(
  api_version = "apps/v1", kind = "Deployment",
  metadata = V1ObjectMeta$new(name = "nginx"),
  spec = V1DeploymentSpec$new(
    replicas = 3L,
    selector = V1LabelSelector$new(match_labels = list(app = "nginx")),
    template = V1PodTemplateSpec$new(
      metadata = V1ObjectMeta$new(labels = list(app = "nginx")),
      spec = V1PodSpec$new(containers = list(
        V1Container$new(name = "nginx", image = "nginx:1.25"))))))
AppsV1Api$new(k$client)$create_namespaced_deployment(
  namespace = "default", body = dep)

Regenerating for a newer Kubernetes

The generated code comes from the OpenAPI spec in tools/gen/spec/. To move to another release, download its spec and run the generator:

curl -L -o tools/gen/spec/swagger.json \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/release-1.31/api/openapi-spec/swagger.json
Rscript tools/gen/generate.R tools/gen/spec/swagger.json R
R CMD build .

It writes about 700 R files of R6 classes and updates the generated part of NAMESPACE (the lines between the sentinel comments).
